equipment: Digital kitchen scale (formulate by weight so the preservative percentage is accurate)
Large glass or stainless mixing bowl and a sturdy spatula
Small container for pre-mixing liquid ingredients (oil, fragrance, preservative)
Spray bottle of 70% isopropyl alcohol for sanitizing tools, bowls, and jars
Wide-mouth PET plastic jars with tight lids (plastic, not glass, for anything used near a shower or tub)
Pipettes or a 0.01 g scale for measuring preservative accurately
Labels listing ingredients and a use-by date
Optional: small scoop or spatula to include with each jar so users never dip wet fingers
safety: Sanitize every bowl, spatula, and jar with 70% isopropyl alcohol and let air-dry before starting; a scrub is only as clean as the dirtiest tool that touched it.

Even though a sugar or salt scrub contains no water, it lives in the shower and WILL get water splashed into it - per Soap Queen and the School of Natural Skincare, an anhydrous product that contacts water in use either needs a preservative or must be scrupulously kept dry, because introduced water lets bacteria and mold grow.

Choose the right preservative chemistry: an oil-soluble broad-spectrum preservative such as Phenonip (used in the heated/oil portion, effective pH 3-8) or Optiphen (about 1-1.5%) suits oil-based scrubs; water-soluble Liquid Germall Plus (0.5%) suits emulsified scrubs. Never exceed the supplier's maximum usage rate.
Salt scrubs sting and can burn on freshly shaved, broken, or irritated skin - label them for body use and warn against use on the face or damaged skin.
Oily scrubs make tub and shower floors dangerously slippery; add a slip-hazard warning to the label.
Keep fragrance/essential oils within dermal safety limits for wash-off body products (typically 1-3% total, checked against IFRA guidance for the specific oil).
Wear gloves while filling jars so skin flora never enters the product.

phases.title: Phase 1 - Choose your exfoliant: sugar vs salt
steps: Pick sugar for a gentler all-purpose scrub: granulated sugar crystals are smaller and rounder, dissolve quickly in warm water, and per the HSCG formulating guidance shared on Soap Queen, sugar scrubs are noticeably more gentle on skin.

Pick salt for a more aggressive, mineral-rich scrub: salt is coarser and, as Marla Bosworth notes in the Soap Queen formulating post, particularly good for skin prone to ingrown hairs, and for rough spots like feet and elbows.

Match grain size to the body part: fine granulated sugar or fine sea salt for regular body use, brown sugar (the softest) for delicate areas, and coarse salts only for feet - avoid coarse Epsom or dead sea chunks on thin skin.
Never substitute salt into a recipe intended for the face, and remember salt partially dissolves into any liquid over time, so very fine salt scrubs can lose grit in storage.

phases.title: Phase 2 - Formulate the oil-to-exfoliant ratio
steps: Start from a base of roughly 75-85% exfoliant and 15-25% oils by weight for a classic crumbly scrub - Soap Queen's Wildflower Honey Sugar Scrub uses 18 oz sugar with 1.5 oz jojoba oil plus 3 oz potassium cocoate, and you can add oil in small increments if you prefer a wetter, more emollient texture.

Choose mostly lightweight, easy-rinsing oils (jojoba, sweet almond, apricot kernel, fractionated coconut); the Soap Queen formulating guide warns that heavy oils and butters leave a greasy film, so blend any heavy oil (coconut, olive) with lighter ones.

Optionally add a foaming or self-emulsifying agent - potassium cocoate (liquid soap paste) or a solid emulsifier - so the scrub rinses clean instead of leaving an oil slick; this also reduces the tub-slip hazard.
Weigh everything and write the batch formula down as percentages, so the preservative can be dosed correctly and the batch can be reproduced.

phases.title: Phase 3 - Mix the liquid portion
steps: In the small sanitized container, combine the carrier oil(s) and any potassium cocoate or emulsifier, stirring until uniform (the mix may turn cloudy and thicken - that is normal).
Add the fragrance or essential oil (about 0.2 oz per 22 oz batch in the Soap Queen honey scrub, i.e. roughly 1%).

Add the preservative to the liquid portion at its recommended rate (for example Optiphen at 1-1.5%, or Phenonip at up to 1% dissolved into slightly warmed oil) and stir thoroughly - the preservative must be fully dispersed in the liquid before it meets the sugar or salt.
If any ingredient was warmed to melt (butters, Phenonip), let the liquid portion cool to lukewarm before combining, so the sugar does not begin dissolving on contact.

phases.title: Phase 4 - Combine, texture-check, and jar
steps: Pour the sugar or salt into the large sanitized bowl and break up any clumps.

Add the liquid ingredients to the exfoliant and fold with a spatula or gloved hands until every crystal is evenly coated - the finished texture should resemble wet sand that holds together loosely when squeezed.
Adjust texture: add more exfoliant a spoonful at a time if the scrub looks oily and soupy, or drizzle in a little more oil if it is dusty and will not hold together.
Spoon the scrub into sanitized jars, pressing gently to remove air pockets, wipe the rims, and seal immediately.
Label each jar with the full ingredient list in descending order, the net weight in ounces and grams, and a use-by date.

finishing: Store jars sealed in a cool, dark, dry place; heat and steam accelerate both microbial growth and oil rancidity, so a shower shelf is the worst long-term home for a scrub.
Advise users (on the label or an insert) to scoop with a dry spoon or spatula - or decant a single use into a small dish before showering - and to keep shower water from spraying into the open jar.
Shelf life: an unpreserved scrub kept perfectly dry should carry a conservative 3-month use-by date; a properly preserved scrub is typically good for 6-12 months.
The real expiry is also limited by the shortest-dated oil in the recipe - a scrub can never outlive the rancidity date of its oldest oil, so note your oils' best-by dates when labeling.
Discard immediately at any sign of off smell (rancid crayon odor), color change, visible mold, or pooled water in the jar.
tips: Formulate and dose by weight, not cups - preservatives only work at the correct percentage of total batch weight (Humblebee & Me's preservative guidance and calculator are built entirely around weight).
Even 'optional' preservation is cheap insurance: Soap Queen adds Optiphen to sugar scrubs precisely because the first shower use splashes water and germs into the jar.
Add vitamin E (about 0.5%) as an antioxidant to slow oil rancidity - remembering that an antioxidant extends oil life but is NOT a preservative and does nothing against bacteria or mold.
Brown sugar makes the gentlest scrub, white granulated is the workhorse, and turbinado or coarse salt is for feet only - offer a texture range rather than one grit for everything.
Small jars beat big jars: a 4 oz jar gets used up before contamination or rancidity can win, while a 16 oz jar sits in the shower for months collecting water.
mistakes: Skipping the preservative because 'there's no water in it' - the product is used with wet hands in a shower, and introduced water plus sugar is a perfect microbial growth medium (this is the single most repeated warning from Soap Queen, Humblebee & Me, and the School of Natural Skincare).
Letting water pool in the jar (wet fingers, shower spray, steamy bathroom storage), which can turn an unpreserved scrub moldy within days.
Using only heavy oils or butters, which leaves a greasy, hard-to-rinse film on skin and a slippery, dangerous tub.
Adding fragrance or preservative to a hot oil mixture (degrading them) or pouring hot liquid over sugar so it melts into syrup - always combine lukewarm.
Measuring by volume and guessing the preservative amount, which almost always under- or over-doses it; both failure modes are unsafe.
